opt4: 'upon Alamoth' (Maiden Sopranos), A Song for the Sons of Korah
correct: 'upon Shoshannim-Eduth' (Lilies of the Testimony), A Psalm of Asaph
explanation: 'Shoshannim-Eduth' means 'Lilies of the Testimony', indicating a lovely melody paired with solemn covenant witness, authored by Asaph. Psalm 80:Title (KJV) - "To the chief Musician upon Shoshannim-Eduth, A Psalm of Asaph."

question: What dynamic instrumental orchestra is summoned for festive celebration in Psalm 81:1-2?
opt1: "Sing aloud unto God our strength: make a joyful noise unto the God of Jacob. Take a psalm, and bring hither the timbrel, the pleasant harp with the psaltery."
opt2: "Praise the Lord with the sound of the horn: make music before the King with stringed instruments and bronze cymbals;"
opt3: "Exalt the Almighty in the sanctuary: sound the double flute and strike the ten-stringed lute in Zion;"
opt4: "Rejoice in the Holy One of Israel: blow the trumpets of victory and play upon the golden lyre with singing;"
correct: "Sing aloud unto God our strength: make a joyful noise unto the God of Jacob. Take a psalm, and bring hither the timbrel, the pleasant harp with the psaltery."
explanation: Festival joy engages the whole ensemble: singing aloud, striking the timbrel (tambourine), and blending the sweet melodies of the harp (kinnor) and psaltery (nevel). Psalm 81:1-2 (KJV) - "Sing aloud unto God our strength: make a joyful noise unto the God of Jacob. Take a psalm, and bring hither the timbrel, the pleasant harp with the psaltery."

question: What festival calendar dates are appointed for blowing the sacred shofar trumpet in Psalm 81:3?
opt1: "Sound the ram's horn at the Passover, at the evening twilight, on the day of unleavened bread;"
opt2: "Blow up the trumpet in the new moon, in the time appointed, on our solemn feast day."
opt3: "Blow the silver clarion on the Day of Atonement, in the tenth day of the month, before the mercy seat;"
opt4: "Sound the trumpet at the sunrise of the sabbath, on every new moon, in the courts of Jerusalem;"
correct: "Blow up the trumpet in the new moon, in the time appointed, on our solemn feast day."
explanation: Directing the blowing of the shofar at the New Moon (Rosh Hashanah / Feast of Trumpets) and at the full moon ('the time appointed' / Feast of Tabernacles). Psalm 81:3 (KJV) - "Blow up the trumpet in the new moon, in the time appointed, on our solemn feast day."

question: What physical burdens of Egyptian slavery did God lift from Israel's shoulders and hands in Psalm 81:6?
opt1: "I broke the iron yoke from his neck: his feet were freed from the clay of the brickfield"
opt2: "I took away the whip of the taskmaster: his hands were released from carrying stone"
opt3: "I removed his shoulder from the burden: his hands were delivered from the pots."
opt4: "I shattered the chains of Pharaoh: his arms were delivered from the oars of the galleys"
correct: "I removed his shoulder from the burden: his hands were delivered from the pots."
explanation: Divine emancipation: God lifted the heavy basket-loads off the slave's chafed shoulders and freed their hands from handling clay brick-making pots. Psalm 81:6 (KJV) - "I removed his shoulder from the burden: his hands were delivered from the pots."

question: From what mysterious theophanic location did God answer Israel, and where did He test them in Psalm 81:7?
opt1: "I spoke unto thee out of the burning bush: I tried thee in the wilderness of Sin. Selah."
opt2: "I answered thy cry from the pillar of cloud: I tested thy faith at the waters of Marah. Selah."
opt3: "I delivered thee out of the depths of the sea: I proved thy heart at the mountain of Horeb. Selah."
opt4: "I answered thee in the secret place of thunder: I proved thee at the waters of Meribah. Selah."
correct: "I answered thee in the secret place of thunder: I proved thee at the waters of Meribah. Selah."
explanation: God revealed His presence amid Sinai's dark thunderous cloud ('the secret place of thunder') and tested their faith during the water crisis at Meribah (Ex 17; Num 20). Psalm 81:7 (KJV) - "Thou calledst in trouble, and I delivered thee; I answered thee in the secret place of thunder: I proved thee at the waters of Meribah. Selah."

question: What famous promise of boundless divine generosity is conditioned upon Israel's faith in Psalm 81:10?
opt1: "I am the LORD thy God, which brought thee out of the land of Egypt: open thy mouth wide, and I will fill it."
opt2: "I am the Almighty that divided the sea: ask of me great things, and I will multiply thy cattle;"
opt3: "I am the God of Abraham thy father: stretch forth thy hands, and I will pour out my blessings;"
opt4: "I am the Holy One of Jacob: call upon my name, and I will give thee the treasures of the heathen;"
correct: "I am the LORD thy God, which brought thee out of the land of Egypt: open thy mouth wide, and I will fill it."
explanation: Like parent birds feeding nestlings, God invites His redeemed children to open their mouths wide in expectant faith, promising to fill every need with abundance. Psalm 81:10 (KJV) - "I am the LORD thy God, which brought thee out of the land of Egypt: open thy mouth wide, and I will fill it."

question: What judicial abandonment overtook Israel when they refused to hearken to God's voice in Psalm 81:11-12?
opt1: "Therefore I delivered them into the hand of the Philistines: and scattered their tribes in the wilderness;"
opt2: "So I gave them up unto their own hearts' lust: and they walked in their own counsels."
opt3: "So my wrath consumed their princes with fire: and they wandered in darkness forty years;"
opt4: "And I withdrew my presence from their camp: and left them to perish by the sword of the Amorite;"
correct: "So I gave them up unto their own hearts' lust: and they walked in their own counsels."
explanation: The most terrible judgment: when sinners persistently reject God's voice, He judicially surrenders them to the unchecked desires of their own corrupt hearts (Rom 1:24). Psalm 81:12 (KJV) - "So I gave them up unto their own hearts' lust: and they walked in their own counsels."

question: What poignant divine lament expresses God's yearning for His people's obedience in Psalm 81:13-14?
opt1: "How often would I have gathered the children of Zion, but ye refused to walk in my statutes;"
opt2: "Would that my heritage had kept my law, then had their peace flowed like an overflowing river;"
opt3: "Oh that my people had hearkened unto me, and Israel had walked in my ways! I should soon have subdued their enemies, and turned my hand against their adversaries."
opt4: "Oh that the seed of Jacob had feared my name, then had their horn been exalted above the heathen;"
correct: "Oh that my people had hearkened unto me, and Israel had walked in my ways! I should soon have subdued their enemies, and turned my hand against their adversaries."
explanation: A glimpse of the grieving heart of God: had Israel simply listened and walked in His ways, Yahweh would have effortlessly and swiftly routed all their foes. Psalm 81:13-14 (KJV) - "Oh that my people had hearkened unto me, and Israel had walked in my ways! I should soon have subdued their enemies, and turned my hand against their adversaries."

question: With what two lavish delicacies would God have satisfied an obedient Israel in Psalm 81:16?
opt1: "With clusters of grapes from Eshcol: and with rich milk and sweet wine from Lebanon"
opt2: "With the choice fat of lambs: and with rivers of pure olive oil from the presses of Zion"
opt3: "With manna from opened heavens: and with sweet pomegranates from the gardens of promise"
opt4: "He should have fed them also with the finest of the wheat: and with honey out of the rock should I have satisfied thee."
correct: "He should have fed them also with the finest of the wheat: and with honey out of the rock should I have satisfied thee."
explanation: Supernatural covenant abundance: nourishing them with the plumpest kernel of wheat ('finest of the wheat') and wild honey dripping even from barren flinty crags ('honey out of the rock'). Psalm 81:16 (KJV) - "He should have fed them also with the finest of the wheat: and with honey out of the rock should I have satisfied thee."

question: What musical instrument or rhythm setting appears in the title of Psalm 81, shared with Psalms 8 and 84?
opt1: 'upon Gittith' (A Psalm of Asaph)

opt4: 'upon Neginoth' (A Stringed Psalm)
correct: 'upon Gittith' (A Psalm of Asaph)
explanation: 'Gittith' is associated either with a musical instrument from Gath or a joyful vintage tune chanted during the autumn grape harvest. Psalm 81:Title (KJV) - "To the chief Musician upon Gittith, A Psalm of Asaph."

question: What unknown language did Joseph encounter in Egypt according to Psalm 81:5?
opt1: "where the hieroglyphs of Pharaoh were written in stone"
opt2: "where I heard a language that I understood not."
opt3: "where the magicians spoke in the tongue of serpents"
opt4: "where foreign taskmasters shouted in an alien voice"
correct: "where I heard a language that I understood not."
explanation: Israel felt the profound alienation of exile in Egypt, dwelling among a foreign culture speaking an unintelligible pagan tongue. Psalm 81:5 (KJV) - "This he ordained in Joseph for a testimony, when he went out through the land of Egypt: where I heard a language that I understood not."

question: What solemn heavenly assize where God presides over human magistrates opens Psalm 82:1?
opt1: "The Lord of hosts sitteth upon the throne of his holiness: he reproveth the kings of the earth;"
opt2: "God standeth in the congregation of the mighty; he judgeth among the gods."
opt3: "The Almighty hath summoned the princes of Israel: he weigheth their judgments in the balances of righteousness;"
opt4: "God hath taken his place in the assembly of the elders: he rebuketh the judges of Zion;"
correct: "God standeth in the congregation of the mighty; he judgeth among the gods."
explanation: God convenes a judicial trial: standing up in the council of rulers and magistrates (titled 'gods' / elohim because they exercise delegated divine authority) to judge their conduct. Psalm 82:1 (KJV) - "God standeth in the congregation of the mighty; he judgeth among the gods."

question: What penetrating indictment of judicial corruption and partiality is delivered in Psalm 82:2?
opt1: "Why take ye bribes from the rich, and pervert the cause of the fatherless? Selah."
opt2: "How darest ye justify the ungodly for silver, and turn aside the poor in the gate? Selah."
opt3: "How long will ye judge unjustly, and accept the persons of the wicked? Selah."
opt4: "Why do ye mock the statutes of Moses, and decree unrighteous decrees against the innocent? Selah."
correct: "How long will ye judge unjustly, and accept the persons of the wicked? Selah."
explanation: God confronts civil magistrates for perverting court equity by showing favoritism to wealthy criminals ('accept the persons of the wicked'). Psalm 82:2 (KJV) - "How long will ye judge unjustly, and accept the persons of the wicked? Selah."

question: What fourfold legal mandate to protect the weak and vulnerable is commanded in Psalm 82:3-4?
opt1: "Pity the stranger and the widow: avenge the blood of the innocent: give bread to the hungry: break the yoke of the oppressor;"
opt2: "Hearken to the cry of the oppressed: vindicate the captive: execute judgment without fear: restore the heritage of the poor;"
opt3: "Open your mouth for the dumb: plead the cause of the destitute: punish the violent: establish righteousness at the gate;"
opt4: "Defend the poor and fatherless: do justice to the afflicted and needy. Deliver the poor and needy: rid them out of the hand of the wicked."
correct: "Defend the poor and fatherless: do justice to the afflicted and needy. Deliver the poor and needy: rid them out of the hand of the wicked."
explanation: The core biblical duty of civil government: actively advocating for the defenseless (orphans, poor, afflicted, needy) and rescuing them from predatory abusers. Psalm 82:3-4 (KJV) - "Defend the poor and fatherless: do justice to the afflicted and needy. Deliver the poor and needy: rid them out of the hand of the wicked."

question: What cosmic and societal catastrophe results from the willful ignorance of corrupt judges in Psalm 82:5?
opt1: "They know not, neither will they understand; they walk on in darkness: all the foundations of the earth are out of course."
opt2: "Their eyes are blinded by bribes; they wander in confusion: the land is filled with violence and tears;"
opt3: "They despise instruction, and harden their necks: the pillars of the sanctuary are shaken into dust;"
opt4: "They follow after vanity, and love deceit: the thrones of the righteous are overturned by the heathen;"
correct: "They know not, neither will they understand; they walk on in darkness: all the foundations of the earth are out of course."
explanation: When the justice system is corrupted by ignorant, darkness-loving judges, the entire moral and societal framework ('all the foundations of the earth') destabilizes into anarchy. Psalm 82:5 (KJV) - "They know not, neither will they understand; they walk on in darkness: all the foundations of the earth are out of course."

question: Which verse from Psalm 82:6 did Jesus quote in John 10:34-36 to defend His claim of divine Sonship?
opt1: "God standeth in the congregation of the mighty; he judgeth among the gods;"
opt2: "I have said, Ye are gods; and all of you are children of the most High."
opt3: "Defend the poor and fatherless: do justice to the afflicted and needy;"
opt4: "Arise, O God, judge the earth: for thou shalt inherit all nations;"
correct: "I have said, Ye are gods; and all of you are children of the most High."
explanation: Jesus cited Psalm 82:6 to argue that if mortal human magistrates commissioned with God's word were titled 'gods', it was not blasphemous for the One sanctified and sent by the Father to say, 'I am the Son of God'. Psalm 82:6 (KJV) - "I have said, Ye are gods; and all of you are children of the most High."

question: What sobering demotion and common mortal death awaits these corrupt magistrates in Psalm 82:7?
opt1: "Yet shall your glory turn to dust, and your souls go down into Sheol"
opt2: "For your sceptres shall be shattered, and ye shall perish like common clay"
opt3: "But ye shall die like men, and fall like one of the princes."
opt4: "Behold, the worms shall devour your flesh, and your crowns shall fade away"
correct: "But ye shall die like men, and fall like one of the princes."
explanation: Despite their elevated titles ('gods'), these magistrates possess zero inherent divinity; they are mortal flesh, destined to die like ordinary humans and fall like any secular prince. Psalm 82:7 (KJV) - "But ye shall die like men, and fall like one of the princes."

question: What worldwide judicial prayer concludes Psalm 82:8?
opt1: "Execute thy judgment, O Lord of hosts: for the kingdoms of the world belong unto thee;"
opt2: "Reign in righteousness, O Most High: for thou hast redeemed thy chosen people from death;"
opt3: "Stand up, O King of Zion: for thy throne endureth throughout all generations;"
opt4: "Arise, O God, judge the earth: for thou shalt inherit all nations."
correct: "Arise, O God, judge the earth: for thou shalt inherit all nations."
explanation: Human courts having failed miserably, the psalmist appeals to the supreme Sovereign to take the bench personally, inheriting and ruling all global nations with perfect justice. Psalm 82:8 (KJV) - "Arise, O God, judge the earth: for thou shalt inherit all nations."

question: What does the Hebrew title 'elohim' ('gods') specifically designate when applied to human beings in Psalm 82:1 and 82:6?
opt1: Duly appointed human civil judges and rulers acting as official representatives and administrators of God's law on earth (Exodus 21:6; 22:8-9)
opt2: Fallen angels and demonic principalities assigned to oversee pagan nations
opt3: Pagan idols carved out of cedar wood and overlaid with silver in Babylon
opt4: The ancient patriarchs Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob reigning in paradise
correct: Duly appointed human civil judges and rulers acting as official representatives and administrators of God's law on earth (Exodus 21:6; 22:8-9)
explanation: In Hebrew jurisprudence, judges were called elohim because they stood in God's place to execute His justice; when they perverted justice, they invited God's direct trial. Psalm 82:1 (KJV) - "God standeth in the congregation of the mighty; he judgeth among the gods."

question: What phrase in Psalm 82:2 describes judicial partiality based on personal bribery or status?
opt1: "receive the gifts of the violent"
opt2: "accept the persons of the wicked"
opt3: "listen to the counsel of the ungodly"
opt4: "justify the deceitful for silver"
correct: "accept the persons of the wicked"
explanation: The Hebrew idiom nasa panim ('lift up the face' / 'accept the person') means granting biased judicial favor to individuals based on their wealth, rank, or bribes rather than facts. Psalm 82:2 (KJV) - "How long will ye judge unjustly, and accept the persons of the wicked? Selah."

question: Who authored Psalm 82 according to its superscription?
opt1: A Psalm of David
opt2: A Song of the Sons of Korah
opt3: A Psalm of Asaph
opt4: A Prayer of Ethan the Ezrahite
correct: A Psalm of Asaph
explanation: Psalm 82 is attributed to Asaph, fitting his prophetic concern for judicial integrity and the moral foundations of society. Psalm 82:Title (KJV) - "A Psalm of Asaph."

question: What triple plea against divine silence in the face of roaring hostile confederacies opens Psalm 83:1-2?
opt1: "Hear my voice, O Lord, in the day of trouble: be not far from me, O my Savior: For the heathen have compassed Zion;"
opt2: "Awake, O God of hosts, why sleepest thou? arise and defend thy people: For the proud have sharpened their swords;"
opt3: "Keep not thou silence, O God: hold not thy peace, and be not still, O God. For, lo, thine enemies make a tumult: and they that hate thee have lifted up the head."
opt4: "Be not silent unto our tears, O King of Jacob: look down from heaven and behold: For an army of nations hath gathered;"
correct: "Keep not thou silence, O God: hold not thy peace, and be not still, O God. For, lo, thine enemies make a tumult: and they that hate thee have lifted up the head."
explanation: Faced with a massive multi-national military encirclement, Asaph pleads with God not to remain a silent, inactive bystander ('Keep not thou silence ... hold not thy peace ... be not still'). Psalm 83:1-2 (KJV) - "Keep not thou silence, O God: hold not thy peace, and be not still, O God. For, lo, thine enemies make a tumult: and they that hate thee have lifted up the head."

question: What genocidal conspiracy against the national existence of Israel is exposed in Psalm 83:3-4?
opt1: "They have formed a league against Zion, saying, Let us burn their sanctuary: that their law may perish from the earth;"

opt3: "They have conspired in secret, saying, Let us divide their inheritance: that none may worship the God of Abraham;"
opt4: "They have taken crafty counsel against thy people, and consulted against thy hidden ones. They have said, Come, and let us cut them off from being a nation; that the name of Israel may be no more in remembrance."
correct: "They have taken crafty counsel against thy people, and consulted against thy hidden ones. They have said, Come, and let us cut them off from being a nation; that the name of Israel may be no more in remembrance."
explanation: Total anti-Semitic annihilation: the confederate alliance schemes not merely to plunder, but to wipe Israel off the map entirely so the very memory of Israel's name is erased. Psalm 83:3-4 (KJV) - "They have taken crafty counsel against thy people, and consulted against thy hidden ones. They have said, Come, and let us cut them off from being a nation; that the name of Israel may be no more in remembrance."

question: Which ten specific nations and tribes comprise the hostile confederacy in Psalm 83:6-8?

opt4: Arameans, Keilah, Ziph, Gath, Ekron, Ashdod, Gaza, Edom, Ammon, and Canaanites
correct: Edom, Ishmaelites, Moab, Hagarenes, Gebal, Ammon, Amalek, Philistines, Tyre, and Assur (Assyria)
explanation: A ten-member hostile encirclement: Transjordan nations, desert nomads, and coastal powers joined by northern imperial superpower Assur. Psalm 83:6-7 (KJV) - "The tabernacles of Edom, and the Ishmaelites; of Moab, and the Hagarenes; Gebal, and Ammon, and Amalek; the Philistines with the inhabitants of Tyre;"

question: What two Judges-era victories at the brook of Kishon does the psalmist invoke in Psalm 83:9-10?
opt1: "Do unto them as unto the five kings of the Amorites, when the sun stood still at Gibeon;"
opt2: "Do unto them as unto the Midianites; as to Sisera, as to Jabin, at the brook of Kison: Which perished at Endor: they became as dung for the earth."
opt3: "Smite them as thou smotest the army of Pharaoh at the Red Sea, and the kings of Bashan;"
opt4: "Overthrow them as thou overthrewest the host of Sennacherib outside the gates of Jerusalem;"
correct: "Do unto them as unto the Midianites; as to Sisera, as to Jabin, at the brook of Kison: Which perished at Endor: they became as dung for the earth."
explanation: Asaph prays that God will duplicate Gideon's victory over Midian and Deborah/Barak's overthrow of Sisera and Jabin at the Kishon river, whose unburied armies fertilized the soil like dung. Psalm 83:9-10 (KJV) - "Do unto them as unto the Midianites; as to Sisera, as to Jabin, at the brook of Kison: Which perished at Endor: they became as dung for the earth."

question: Which four Midianite commanders from the Book of Judges are named in Psalm 83:11?
opt1: Sihon and Og (kings), and Balak and Balaam (princes)

opt4: Eglon and Sisera (rulers), and Adonibezek and Nahash (captains)
correct: Oreb and Zeeb (princes), and Zebah and Zalmunna (kings)
explanation: Gideon slew Midianite generals Oreb ('Raven') and Zeeb ('Wolf') at the winepress and rock (Judg 7:25), and executed Midianite kings Zebah and Zalmunna (Judg 8:21). Psalm 83:11 (KJV) - "Make their nobles like Oreb, and like Zeeb: yea, all their princes as Zebah, and as Zalmunna:"

question: What sacrilegious motive driving the confederacy is exposed in Psalm 83:12?
opt1: "Who said, Let us carry away the ark of the covenant into our temples"
opt2: "Who said, Let us make the children of Judah our perpetual bondservants"

correct: "Who said, Let us take to ourselves the houses of God in possession."
explanation: Their brazen insolence targeted God's personal property: plotting to seize the sacred sanctuaries and grazing pastures ('houses of God') of Yahweh for themselves. Psalm 83:12 (KJV) - "Who said, Let us take to ourselves the houses of God in possession."

question: What dynamic similes of windblown tumbleweed, hurricane, and mountain wildfire are invoked in Psalm 83:13-15?
opt1: "O my God, make them like a wheel; as the stubble before the wind. As the fire burneth a wood, and as the flame setteth the mountains on fire; So persecute them with thy tempest, and make them afraid with thy storm."
opt2: "O Lord, scatter them like dust before the chariot; as dry chaff in the whirlwind: let thy lightning consume their tents;"
opt3: "Make them as melting wax before the furnace; as foam upon the raging sea: overtake them with sudden destruction;"
opt4: "Let them vanish like morning mist; as withered grass upon the housetops: drown their host in the overflowing torrent;"
correct: "O my God, make them like a wheel; as the stubble before the wind. As the fire burneth a wood, and as the flame setteth the mountains on fire; So persecute them with thy tempest, and make them afraid with thy storm."
explanation: Asaph prays that foes be spun like whirling tumbleweeds (galgal / 'a wheel'), blown like dry stubble, and consumed like a raging forest wildfire racing across mountain slopes. Psalm 83:13-15 (KJV) - "O my God, make them like a wheel; as the stubble before the wind. As the fire burneth a wood, and as the flame setteth the mountains on fire; So persecute them with thy tempest, and make them afraid with thy storm."

question: What redemptive and evangelistic purpose underlies the humiliation of the enemies in Psalm 83:16?
opt1: "Smite their princes with blindness; that they may bring silver to the sanctuary of Zion"
opt2: "Fill their faces with shame; that they may seek thy name, O LORD."
opt3: "Shatter their iron chariots; that they may bow down before the king of Judah"
opt4: "Break their proud bows; that they may confess the covenant of Abraham"
correct: "Fill their faces with shame; that they may seek thy name, O LORD."
explanation: The ultimate goal of divine discipline is not vindictive annihilation, but redemptive awakening: filling their faces with humiliating defeat so that they seek the saving Name of Yahweh. Psalm 83:16 (KJV) - "Fill their faces with shame; that they may seek thy name, O LORD."

question: What grand theological climax and revelation of God's supreme Name concludes Psalm 83:18?
opt1: "That all nations may confess that God is the Creator of heaven and earth and King of kings"
opt2: "So that the kingdoms of the world may fear the Holy One of Israel and worship at his holy hill"
opt3: "That men may know that thou, whose name alone is JEHOVAH, art the most high over all the earth."
opt4: "And all flesh shall declare that the Lord of hosts reigneth in Mount Zion for ever and ever"
correct: "That men may know that thou, whose name alone is JEHOVAH, art the most high over all the earth."
explanation: One of only four verses in the KJV Old Testament where the sacred covenant name JEHOVAH is fully rendered in all caps (along with Ex 6:3; Ps 83:18; Isa 12:2; 26:4), demonstrating His cosmic supremacy as Elyon ('the most high over all the earth'). Psalm 83:18 (KJV) - "That men may know that thou, whose name alone is JEHOVAH, art the most high over all the earth."

question: What special milestone does Psalm 83 represent in the overall structure of the Book of Psalms?

correct: It is the final psalm of the 12-psalm Asaphic collection (Psalms 50, 73-83)
explanation: Psalm 83 concludes the famous Asaph collection (which began in Psalm 50 and continued through Psalms 73-83), highlighting Asaph's prophetic focus on national history and God's sovereignty. Psalm 83:Title (KJV) - "A Song or Psalm of Asaph."

question: What exclamation of delight and total soul-thirst for God's sanctuary opens Psalm 84:1-2?
opt1: "How glorious is thy temple, O King of Zion! My spirit rejoiceth in the courts of praise: my soul thirsteth for the rock of salvation;"

opt3: "How excellent are thy dwelling places, O God of Jacob! My eyes weep for the courts of peace: my tongue blesseth the Holy One;"
opt4: "How amiable are thy tabernacles, O LORD of hosts! My soul longeth, yea, even fainteth for the courts of the LORD: my heart and my flesh crieth out for the living God."
correct: "How amiable are thy tabernacles, O LORD of hosts! My soul longeth, yea, even fainteth for the courts of the LORD: my heart and my flesh crieth out for the living God."
explanation: The pilgrim bursts into ecstatic adoration: God's tabernacles are supremely lovely ('amiable'), causing the entire person - soul, heart, and physical flesh - to faint with longing for the living God. Psalm 84:1-2 (KJV) - "How amiable are thy tabernacles, O LORD of hosts! My soul longeth, yea, even fainteth for the courts of the LORD: my heart and my flesh crieth out for the living God."

question: What small, humble birds find a secure sanctuary and nest near God's altars in Psalm 84:3?

opt2: "Even the wild dove hath built a shelter in the cedar beams, and the fledgling in the holy place;"
opt3: "Behold, the eagle maketh her perch upon the battlements, and the turtledove beneath the altar of incense;"
opt4: "Yea, the harmless sparrow resteth under the wings of the cherubim, and the swallow in the courts of Zion;"
correct: "Yea, the sparrow hath found an house, and the swallow a nest for herself, where she may lay her young, even thine altars, O LORD of hosts, my King, and my God."
explanation: Envious of tiny, insignificant birds, the pilgrim notes that the frail sparrow and restless swallow find permanent homes and raise their young right beside the sacrificial altars of Yahweh Sabaoth. Psalm 84:3 (KJV) - "Yea, the sparrow hath found an house, and the swallow a nest for herself, where she may lay her young, even thine altars, O LORD of hosts, my King, and my God."

question: What perpetual occupation marks the beatitude of temple dwellers in Psalm 84:4?
opt1: "Blessed are the priests that minister at thine altar: they shall behold thy glory for ever. Selah."
opt2: "Blessed are they that dwell in thy house: they will be still praising thee. Selah."
opt3: "Blessed are the Levites that watch the sacred gates: their joy shall never depart. Selah."

correct: "Blessed are they that dwell in thy house: they will be still praising thee. Selah."
explanation: Permanent residency in God's presence produces unending, spontaneous worship: those who abide in His house 'will be still [continually] praising thee'. Psalm 84:4 (KJV) - "Blessed are they that dwell in thy house: they will be still praising thee. Selah."

question: How do pilgrims transform arid adversity as they journey toward Zion in Psalm 84:5-6?

opt4: "Blessed is the congregation of Jacob: walking through the valley of shadow, the Lord is their shepherd;"
correct: "Blessed is the man whose strength is in thee; in whose heart are the ways of them. Who passing through the valley of Baca make it a well; the rain also filleth the pools."
explanation: The valley of Baca ('weeping' / arid balsam trees) represents barren trials; yet pilgrims anchored in divine strength turn places of tears into bubbling springs of spiritual refreshment. Psalm 84:5-6 (KJV) - "Blessed is the man whose strength is in thee; in whose heart are the ways of them. Who passing through the valley of Baca make it a well; the rain also filleth the pools."

question: What paradoxical increase of energy marks the Zion pilgrims' journey in Psalm 84:7?
opt1: "Their youth is renewed like the eagle, until they stand within the golden gates of Jerusalem"

correct: "They go from strength to strength, every one of them in Zion appeareth before God."
explanation: Unlike ordinary physical journeys that induce fatigue, the spiritual pilgrimage to Zion infuses escalating divine stamina: going 'from strength to strength' until standing safely before God. Psalm 84:7 (KJV) - "They go from strength to strength, every one of them in Zion appeareth before God."

question: What famous comparative valuation of a single day in God's presence is declared in Psalm 84:10?

opt4: "For one morning in thy presence exceedeth a lifetime of earthly pomp: I had rather wash the feet of the priests in Jerusalem;"
correct: "For a day in thy courts is better than a thousand. I had rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God, than to dwell in the tents of wickedness."
explanation: One solitary day in communion with God eclipses a thousand days of secular pleasure; standing as a humble threshold-guard (doorkeeper) in God's house far surpasses residing in luxury inside ungodly palaces. Psalm 84:10 (KJV) - "For a day in thy courts is better than a thousand. I had rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God, than to dwell in the tents of wickedness."

question: What celestial and protective metaphors are ascribed to God, and what boundless promise is given in Psalm 84:11?

explanation: God is our Sun (imparting life, warmth, and light) and our Shield (providing total defense); He bestows both saving grace in this life and celestial glory hereafter, withholding zero good things from the upright. Psalm 84:11 (KJV) - "For the LORD God is a sun and shield: the LORD will give grace and glory: no good thing will he withhold from them that walk uprightly."

question: What final beatitude seals the entire message of Psalm 84 in verse 12?

question: Who authored Psalm 84 according to its superscription, and to what musical instrument was it set?

question: What three distinct beatitudes ('Blessed') structure the spiritual progression of Psalm 84?

question: What threefold recollection of past national restoration and forgiveness opens Psalm 85:1-2?

explanation: Post-exilic thanksgiving recounts God's historical favor: returning the exiles of Jacob, forgiving their iniquity, and completely covering (atoning for) all their sins. Psalm 85:1-2 (KJV) - "Lord, thou hast been favourable unto thy land: thou hast brought back the captivity of Jacob. Thou hast forgiven the iniquity of thy people, thou hast covered all their sin. Selah."

question: What famous revival prayer links spiritual quickening with holy joy in Psalm 85:6?

question: What resolution to hear God's oracle of peace is paired with a warning against backsliding in Psalm 85:8?
opt1: "I will attend unto the voice of the sanctuary: for he will proclaim righteousness: but let none transgress his statutes;"

explanation: God's promised covenant shalom ('peace') is unconditional in its source but demands holy vigilance: saints must never abuse grace by returning to their former sinful folly. Psalm 85:8 (KJV) - "I will hear what God the LORD will speak: for he will speak peace unto his people, and to his saints: but let them not turn again to folly."

question: What magnificent personification of divine attributes reconciles at the Cross in Psalm 85:10?

correct: "Mercy and truth are met together; righteousness and peace have kissed each other."
explanation: A breathtaking theological convergence: at the Cross, God's unrelenting Righteousness and Truth satisfy divine justice, while His tender Mercy and Peace embrace the redeemed sinner. Psalm 85:10 (KJV) - "Mercy and truth are met together; righteousness and peace have kissed each other."

question: How do heaven and earth interact in mutual celebration of redemption in Psalm 85:11?

opt4: "Faithfulness shall sprout like a green vine; and holiness shall illuminate the nations"
correct: "Truth shall spring out of the earth; and righteousness shall look down from heaven."
explanation: A glorious reconciliation of creation: human fidelity and Truth sprout upward like fertile harvest shoots from earth, while heavenly Righteousness smiles downward like radiant sunshine. Psalm 85:11 (KJV) - "Truth shall spring out of the earth; and righteousness shall look down from heaven."

question: What royal herald goes before God to pave the way of His footsteps in Psalm 85:13?

correct: "Righteousness shall go before him; and shall set us in the way of his steps."

question: To whom is God's salvation near, and what indwelling reality results in Psalm 85:9?

opt4: "His mercy is extended to the seed of Jacob; that righteousness may cover the earth"

explanation: The God-fearing experience immediate proximity to divine salvation, ensuring that the visible Shekinah glory of God permanently inhabits their commonwealth. Psalm 85:9 (KJV) - "Surely his salvation is nigh them that fear him; that glory may dwell in our land."

question: What physical agricultural blessing accompanies spiritual restoration in Psalm 85:12?

question: What urgent petition pleads for the cessation of divine displeasure in Psalm 85:4?

question: Who authored Psalm 85 according to its superscription?

question: What dual basis of personal helplessness and covenant devotion opens David's prayer in Psalm 86:1-2?

correct: "Bow down thine ear, O LORD, hear me: for I am poor and needy. Preserve my soul; for I am holy: O thou my God, save thy servant that trusteth in thee."

Psalm 86:1-2 (KJV) - "Bow down thine ear, O LORD, hear me: for I am poor and needy. Preserve my soul; for I am holy: O thou my God, save thy servant that trusteth in thee."

question: What triple declaration of God's forgiving character and abounding mercy is confessed in Psalm 86:5?

opt3: "For thou, Lord, art good, and ready to forgive; and plenteous in mercy unto all them that call upon thee."
opt4: "Seeing that the Almighty is full of compassion; and ready to heal the broken in heart;"
