explanation: A cornerstone attribute of God: He is inherently good, eager ('ready') to pardon, and overflowing in plenteous covenant mercy (hesed) to all who pray. Psalm 86:5 (KJV) - "For thou, Lord, art good, and ready to forgive; and plenteous in mercy unto all them that call upon thee."

question: How does David affirm the absolute incomparability and exclusivity of God in Psalm 86:8 and 86:10?
opt1: "Who is like unto the Lord in the heavens? none can stand before his throne: for he is King above all gods;"
opt2: "The idols of the heathen are silver and gold: but our God hath created the universe: he alone is Holy;"
opt3: "All the gods of the nations are vanity: but Yahweh is clothed with majesty: he alone ruleth the earth;"
opt4: "Among the gods there is none like unto thee, O Lord; neither are there any works like unto thy works ... For thou art great, and doest wondrous things: thou art God alone."
correct: "Among the gods there is none like unto thee, O Lord; neither are there any works like unto thy works ... For thou art great, and doest wondrous things: thou art God alone."
explanation: Radical monotheism: no pagan deity compares to Yahweh in nature or miraculous deeds; He is 'God alone' without rival. Psalm 86:8, 10 (KJV) - "Among the gods there is none like unto thee, O Lord; neither are there any works like unto thy works ... For thou art great, and doest wondrous things: thou art God alone."

question: What universal eschatological worship of all created nations is prophesied in Psalm 86:9?
opt1: "All nations whom thou hast made shall come and worship before thee, O Lord; and shall glorify thy name."
opt2: "All the kingdoms of the earth shall bring tribute to Zion; and kings shall fall down at his footstool;"
opt3: "Every tribe under heaven shall confess his righteousness; and all flesh shall praise the King of glory;"
opt4: "The gentiles shall flow into the holy temple; and the islands of the sea shall proclaim his salvation;"
correct: "All nations whom thou hast made shall come and worship before thee, O Lord; and shall glorify thy name."
explanation: Because God created all ethnic peoples, history marches toward a global climax where every nation bows in genuine worship, glorifying Yahweh's Name (Rev 15:4). Psalm 86:9 (KJV) - "All nations whom thou hast made shall come and worship before thee, O Lord; and shall glorify thy name."

question: What famous prayer for single-minded spiritual devotion and obedience is found in Psalm 86:11?
opt1: "Guide my footsteps in thy law, O God; I will keep thy testimonies: purify my mind to love thy word;"
opt2: "Teach me thy way, O LORD; I will walk in thy truth: unite my heart to fear thy name."
opt3: "Lead me in the path of righteousness, O Lord; I will meditate on thy statutes: establish my soul in peace;"
opt4: "Instruct my heart in wisdom, O Most High; I will obey thy commandments: fix my spirit upon Mount Zion;"
correct: "Teach me thy way, O LORD; I will walk in thy truth: unite my heart to fear thy name."
explanation: Recognizing the danger of a divided, distracted soul, David asks God to integrate all his affections into an undivided whole: 'unite my heart to fear thy name'. Psalm 86:11 (KJV) - "Teach me thy way, O LORD; I will walk in thy truth: unite my heart to fear thy name."

question: From what deep subterranean realm of death did God's great mercy deliver David's soul in Psalm 86:13?
opt1: "the mouth of the lion"
opt2: "the snare of the fowler"
opt3: "the lowest hell"
opt4: "the pit of corruption"
correct: "the lowest hell"
explanation: David praises God for delivering him from Sheol tachtiyyah ('the lowest hell' / deepest depths of the grave), celebrating rescue from physical and spiritual destruction. Psalm 86:13 (KJV) - "For great is thy mercy toward me: and thou hast delivered my soul from the lowest hell."

question: What verbatim recitation of the classic Exodus 34:6 revelation of divine character appears in Psalm 86:15?
opt1: "The Lord God omnipotent reigneth, holy and true, forgiving iniquity and visiting the ungodly with wrath;"
opt2: "For the Almighty is righteous in all his ways, loving unto his people, and unchangeable in his covenant;"
opt3: "The Lord is my light and my salvation, keeping mercy for thousands, and showing lovingkindness to Israel;"
opt4: "But thou, O Lord, art a God full of compassion, and gracious, long suffering, and plenteous in mercy and truth."
correct: "But thou, O Lord, art a God full of compassion, and gracious, long suffering, and plenteous in mercy and truth."
explanation: David quotes the foundational Old Testament creed of divine grace revealed to Moses on Mount Sinai (Ex 34:6). Psalm 86:15 (KJV) - "But thou, O Lord, art a God full of compassion, and gracious, long suffering, and plenteous in mercy and truth."

question: How does David designate himself in his humble prayer for divine strength in Psalm 86:16?
opt1: "the son of thine handmaid"
opt2: "the anointed of thy sanctuary"
opt3: "the prince of the house of Judah"
opt4: "the shepherd of Bethlehem"
correct: "the son of thine handmaid"
explanation: Designating himself 'the son of thine handmaid' emphasizes humble, inherited covenant servanthood: born into God's household of a godly mother, belonging wholly to the Master. Psalm 86:16 (KJV) - "O turn unto me, and have mercy upon me; give thy strength unto thy servant, and save the son of thine handmaid."

question: What specific request for public vindication against enemies concludes Psalm 86:17?
opt1: "Send forth an angel of salvation; that the ungodly may tremble and flee: for thou art my high tower;"
opt2: "Shew me a token for good; that they which hate me may see it, and be ashamed: because thou, LORD, hast holpen me, and comforted me."
opt3: "Lift up the light of thy countenance; that all mine adversaries may perish: for thou hast established my throne;"
opt4: "Break the weapons of the violent; that the heathen may know thy power: for thou hast delivered my soul;"
correct: "Shew me a token for good; that they which hate me may see it, and be ashamed: because thou, LORD, hast holpen me, and comforted me."
explanation: David asks for a visible 'token for good' (an unmistakable sign of divine favor) that will silence his mockers and put persecutors to shame. Psalm 86:17 (KJV) - "Shew me a token for good; that they which hate me may see it, and be ashamed: because thou, LORD, hast holpen me, and comforted me."

question: What unique distinction belongs to Psalm 86 in the overall structure of Book III of the Psalter (Psalms 73-89)?
opt1: It is the only psalm written in the Aramaic language
opt2: It is the longest chapter in Book III of the Psalter
opt3: It is the only psalm in Book III explicitly titled 'A Prayer of David'
opt4: It is the only psalm with an acrostic alphabet structure in Book III
correct: It is the only psalm in Book III explicitly titled 'A Prayer of David'
explanation: Book III is dominated by Asaph and the sons of Korah; Psalm 86 stands as a solitary Davidic diamond, titled 'A Prayer of David'. Psalm 86:Title (KJV) - "A Prayer of David."

question: Where is God's foundation established, and what does the LORD love more than all dwellings of Jacob in Psalm 87:1-2?
opt1: "His throne is set upon Mount Moriah. The Almighty delighteth in the temple of Jerusalem more than in Shiloh;"
opt2: "His sanctuary is founded upon the rock of ages. The Lord blesseth the courts of David above all the tents of Israel;"
opt3: "His foundation is in the holy mountains. The LORD loveth the gates of Zion more than all the dwellings of Jacob."
opt4: "His glory dwelleth in the holy hills. The Holy One of Jacob honoreth Mount Zion above all the cities of Judah;"
correct: "His foundation is in the holy mountains. The LORD loveth the gates of Zion more than all the dwellings of Jacob."
explanation: Mount Zion, anchored in the sacred ridge of Jerusalem's holy mountains, is loved by God above any other residential dwelling place across all the twelve tribes. Psalm 87:1-2 (KJV) - "His foundation is in the holy mountains. The LORD loveth the gates of Zion more than all the dwellings of Jacob."

question: What famous exclamation celebrating the renown of the city of God is declared in Psalm 87:3?
opt1: "Beautiful for situation is the mountain of the Lord. Selah."
opt2: "Great is the peace of Jerusalem, the palace of the King. Selah."
opt3: "Holy is Zion, the perfection of beauty throughout all the earth. Selah."
opt4: "Glorious things are spoken of thee, O city of God. Selah."
correct: "Glorious things are spoken of thee, O city of God. Selah."
explanation: John Newton's beloved hymn 'Glorious things of thee are spoken, Zion, city of our God' draws directly from this inspired, ecstatic verse. Psalm 87:3 (KJV) - "Glorious things are spoken of thee, O city of God. Selah."

question: Which historic pagan empires and surrounding nations are enumerated in the international citizen roll in Psalm 87:4?
opt1: Rahab (Egypt) and Babylon, Philistia, Tyre, with Ethiopia
opt2: Assyria and Persia, Damascus, Moab, with Ammon
opt3: Rome and Greece, Edom, Midian, with Sheba
opt4: Chaldea and Media, Amalek, Gebal, with Tarshish
correct: Rahab (Egypt) and Babylon, Philistia, Tyre, with Ethiopia
explanation: The most fierce historical persecutors (Egypt/Rahab, Babylon, Philistia, merchant Tyre, and distant Cush/Ethiopia) are included in Zion's citizenship. Psalm 87:4 (KJV) - "I will make mention of Rahab and Babylon to them that know me: behold Philistia, and Tyre, with Ethiopia; this man was born there."

question: What astounding spiritual status is conferred upon foreign converts regarding Zion in Psalm 87:4-5?
opt1: "they shall be adopted as servants: and the kings of the earth shall bring tribute"
opt2: "this man was born there ... This and that man was born in her: and the highest himself shall establish her."
opt3: "these strangers shall dwell within her gates: and the high priest shall sprinkle them"
opt4: "they shall offer sacrifices upon her altar: and the elders shall teach them the law"
correct: "this man was born there ... This and that man was born in her: and the highest himself shall establish her."
explanation: A breathtaking prophecy of spiritual regeneration: converted Gentiles are not treated as second-class aliens, but receive full native-born birthright status in Zion ('born in her'). Psalm 87:4-5 (KJV) - "behold Philistia, and Tyre, with Ethiopia; this man was born there. And of Zion it shall be said, This and that man was born in her: and the highest himself shall establish her."

question: What divine celestial census is conducted by Yahweh in Psalm 87:6?
opt1: "The Almighty shall register the tribes of Jacob, when he numbereth his saints in the book of life. Selah."
opt2: "The Lord of hosts shall record the names of the righteous, when he gathereth his flock into Jerusalem. Selah."
opt3: "The LORD shall count, when he writeth up the people, that this man was born there. Selah."
opt4: "The King shall count his jewels, when he inscribeth the redeemed in the golden roll of Zion. Selah."
correct: "The LORD shall count, when he writeth up the people, that this man was born there. Selah."
explanation: God keeps His own municipal registry: when He compiles the eternal census roll of the redeemed, He enters alongside each Gentile believer's name: 'Born in Zion!'. Psalm 87:6 (KJV) - "The LORD shall count, when he writeth up the people, that this man was born there. Selah."

question: What joyful musical climax and confession of divine life closes Psalm 87:7?
opt1: "The priests and the Levites shall sound the silver trumpets: our life is hidden in God"
opt2: "The virgins with timbrels and the harpers shall rejoice: our salvation floweth from Zion"
opt3: "All the redeemed shall dance before the ark: our fountain of joy is in the Lord"
opt4: "As well the singers as the players on instruments shall be there: all my springs are in thee."
correct: "As well the singers as the players on instruments shall be there: all my springs are in thee."
explanation: Vocalists and instrumentalists join in an ecstatic festival chorus, confessing that every life-giving fountain and refreshing spring of joy and salvation resides in God alone ('all my springs are in thee'). Psalm 87:7 (KJV) - "As well the singers as the players on instruments shall be there: all my springs are in thee."

question: What is the symbolic meaning of the name 'Rahab' in Psalm 87:4?
opt1: A poetic moniker for the nation of Egypt (symbolizing fierce, ferocious pride and chaos)
opt2: The innkeeper woman of Jericho who hid the two Hebrew spies
opt3: The mythical sea serpent slain by Nimrod at Babel
opt4: A queen of Sheba who brought camel caravans to Solomon
correct: A poetic moniker for the nation of Egypt (symbolizing fierce, ferocious pride and chaos)
explanation: In biblical poetry, 'Rahab' (literally 'arrogance / bluster / dragon') is an established code name for the proud empire of Egypt (see Psalm 89:10; Isaiah 51:9). Psalm 87:4 (KJV) - "I will make mention of Rahab and Babylon to them that know me ..."

question: Why does Psalm 87:1 use the plural expression 'the holy mountains'?
opt1: It refers to the mountains of Sinai and Horeb in Arabia
opt2: Because Jerusalem is situated upon a cluster of interconnected sacred hills (Moriah, Zion, Ophel, Bezetha) ringed by mountains (Psalm 125:2)
opt3: It includes the twin peaks of Mount Ebal and Mount Gerizim
opt4: It encompasses Mount Carmel, Mount Tabor, and Mount Hermon
correct: Because Jerusalem is situated upon a cluster of interconnected sacred hills (Moriah, Zion, Ophel, Bezetha) ringed by mountains (Psalm 125:2)
explanation: Jerusalem is set upon a mountain ridge (Mount Moriah and Mount Zion) surrounded by defensive hills, all consecrated by God's dwelling presence. Psalm 87:1 (KJV) - "His foundation is in the holy mountains."

question: Who authored Psalm 87 according to its superscription?
opt1: A Psalm of Asaph
opt2: A Song of Ascents of David
opt3: A Psalm or Song for the sons of Korah
opt4: A Maschil of Ethan the Ezrahite
correct: A Psalm or Song for the sons of Korah
explanation: Composed by the guild of the sons of Korah, whose deep love for the temple gates (they were temple gatekeepers, 1 Chron 9:19) shines in this city-hymn. Psalm 87:Title (KJV) - "A Psalm or Song for the sons of Korah."

question: What New Testament theological truth is foreshadowed in Psalm 87's vision of Zion?
opt1: The rebuilding of the second temple by Zerubbabel after the exile
opt2: The military conquests of the Maccabean revolt over the Seleucid kings
opt3: The physical relocation of all Gentile nations to Judean territory
opt4: The Heavenly Jerusalem and the Church as the global spiritual birthplace of all believers through the new birth (Galatians 4:26; Hebrews 12:22)
correct: The Heavenly Jerusalem and the Church as the global spiritual birthplace of all believers through the new birth (Galatians 4:26; Hebrews 12:22)
explanation: Paul in Galatians 4:26 speaks of 'Jerusalem which is above ... which is the mother of us all', fulfilling Psalm 87's vision of citizens born from every nation into Zion. Psalm 87:5 (KJV) - "And of Zion it shall be said, This and that man was born in her: and the highest himself shall establish her."

question: What relentless nocturnal and daytime prayer opens Psalm 88:1-2?
opt1: "Hear my groaning, O Lord, in the dark night: bow down thine ear unto my tears;"
opt2: "Out of the deep have I called unto thee, O Almighty: hear my voice in the morning watch;"
opt3: "Look upon my affliction, O King of Israel: let my supplication enter into thy presence;"
opt4: "O LORD God of my salvation, I have cried day and night before thee: Let my prayer come before thee: incline thine ear unto my cry;"
correct: "O LORD God of my salvation, I have cried day and night before thee: Let my prayer come before thee: incline thine ear unto my cry;"
explanation: Even in the darkest despair, faith anchors in the single ray of light in the entire psalm: addressing Yahweh as 'the God of my salvation' in unceasing day-and-night prayer. Psalm 88:1-2 (KJV) - "O LORD God of my salvation, I have cried day and night before thee: Let my prayer come before thee: incline thine ear unto my cry;"

question: What death-like state and grim military metaphor describe the sufferer in Psalm 88:4-5?
opt1: "I am counted with them that go down into the pit: I am as a man that hath no strength: Free among the dead, like the slain that lie in the grave, whom thou rememberest no more: and they are cut off from thy hand."
opt2: "I am become as dry bones in the valley: like soldiers fallen in battle, forgotten by their king;"
opt3: "My soul is cast into Sheol: like an unburied carcass trampled in the mire, abandoned by all men;"
opt4: "I wander among sepulchres without breath: like a prisoner bound in chains of iron, cut off from light;"
correct: "I am counted with them that go down into the pit: I am as a man that hath no strength: Free among the dead, like the slain that lie in the grave, whom thou rememberest no more: and they are cut off from thy hand."
explanation: The sufferer feels discarded, 'free among the dead' (emancipated from the duties and relationships of the living like a corpse lying in a mass battlefield grave). Psalm 88:4-5 (KJV) - "I am counted with them that go down into the pit: I am as a man that hath no strength: Free among the dead, like the slain that lie in the grave, whom thou rememberest no more: and they are cut off from thy hand."

question: How does the psalmist describe the subterranean darkness and crushing weight of God's wrath in Psalm 88:6-7?
opt1: "Thou hast plunged me into the abyss: thick darkness compasseth my soul: the storm of thy fury beateth upon my head. Selah."
opt2: "Thou hast laid me in the lowest pit, in darkness, in the deeps. Thy wrath lieth hard upon me, and thou hast afflicted me with all thy waves. Selah."
opt3: "Thou hast cast me into outer darkness: my bones are crushed beneath the waves of thy judgment. Selah."
opt4: "Thou hast shut me in the subterranean vault: thy wrath burneth like sulfur: the floods of death overwhelm me. Selah."
correct: "Thou hast laid me in the lowest pit, in darkness, in the deeps. Thy wrath lieth hard upon me, and thou hast afflicted me with all thy waves. Selah."
explanation: The ultimate isolation: buried in the 'lowest pit', smothered in pitch darkness, feeling the relentless, crushing breakers ('waves') of divine wrath pounding over his soul. Psalm 88:6-7 (KJV) - "Thou hast laid me in the lowest pit, in darkness, in the deeps. Thy wrath lieth hard upon me, and thou hast afflicted me with all thy waves. Selah."

question: What total social isolation and repulsive quarantine are lamented in Psalm 88:8?
opt1: "My lovers and my friends stand afar off: they mock my affliction and despise my tears"
opt2: "My brethren have forgotten my name: they flee from my face as from a leper in the street"
opt3: "Thou hast put away mine acquaintance far from me; thou hast made me an abomination unto them: I am shut up, and I cannot come forth."
opt4: "Mine elders have cast me out of the congregation: they close their gates against my cry"
correct: "Thou hast put away mine acquaintance far from me; thou hast made me an abomination unto them: I am shut up, and I cannot come forth."
explanation: Total ostracism (likely suffering from chronic leprosy or contagious illness): companions recoil from him as an 'abomination', permanently quarantined in solitary confinement. Psalm 88:8 (KJV) - "Thou hast put away mine acquaintance far from me; thou hast made me an abomination unto them: I am shut up, and I cannot come forth."

question: What four rhetorical questions in Psalm 88:10-12 argue that God's wonders and praises are extinguished in the grave?
opt1: "Can the dust give thanks unto the Lord? shall the worms declare thy holiness? Can the pit confess thy mercy? shall the dead proclaim thy name? Selah."
opt2: "Doth Sheol sing of thy power? shall the shadow of death magnify thy grace? Can the tomb reveal thy glory? shall corruption declare thy salvation? Selah."
opt3: "Wilt thou speak to those in the dust? shall the sepulchre echo with praise? Can the departed behold thy light? shall the dead rejoice in Zion? Selah."
opt4: "Wilt thou shew wonders to the dead? shall the dead arise and praise thee? Selah. Shall thy lovingkindness be declared in the grave? or thy faithfulness in destruction? Shall thy wonders be known in the dark? and thy righteousness in the land of forgetfulness?"
correct: "Wilt thou shew wonders to the dead? shall the dead arise and praise thee? Selah. Shall thy lovingkindness be declared in the grave? or thy faithfulness in destruction? Shall thy wonders be known in the dark? and thy righteousness in the land of forgetfulness?"
explanation: Heman marshals a desperate defense: if God allows him to die, the Lord loses an active voice of praise; dead corpses in Sheol cannot proclaim God's lovingkindness. Psalm 88:10-11 (KJV) - "Wilt thou shew wonders to the dead? shall the dead arise and praise thee? Selah. Shall thy lovingkindness be declared in the grave? or thy faithfulness in destruction?"

question: How early in the morning does the psalmist meet God with his desperate cries in Psalm 88:13?
opt1: "But unto thee have I cried, O LORD; and in the morning shall my prayer prevent thee."
opt2: "In the dawn watch will I lift up my voice: before the sun ariseth will I seek thy face"
opt3: "Early will I pour out my soul: before the morning sacrifice shall my cry reach heaven"
opt4: "At daybreak shall my tears flow: before the light appeareth will I call upon thy name"
correct: "But unto thee have I cried, O LORD; and in the morning shall my prayer prevent thee."
explanation: Unbroken persistence: despite feeling utterly abandoned, Heman rises before the dawn; his morning prayer 'prevents' (comes out early to meet) God at daybreak. Psalm 88:13 (KJV) - "But unto thee have I cried, O LORD; and in the morning shall my prayer prevent thee."

question: How long has the psalmist endured this chronic affliction and terror according to Psalm 88:15?
opt1: "For forty years have I wept in the wilderness: my soul is broken under thy rod"
opt2: "I am afflicted and ready to die from my youth up: while I suffer thy terrors I am distracted."
opt3: "From the days of my childhood have I walked in darkness: my spirit is consumed with grief"
opt4: "All my life have I borne the reproach of the ungodly: my heart is overwhelmed with sorrow"
correct: "I am afflicted and ready to die from my youth up: while I suffer thy terrors I am distracted."
explanation: This was not an acute, temporary crisis: Heman had suffered debilitating, chronic illness and mental distress from boyhood ('from my youth up'), distracted and unhinged by divine terrors. Psalm 88:15 (KJV) - "I am afflicted and ready to die from my youth up: while I suffer thy terrors I am distracted."

question: What chilling and solitary word concludes Psalm 88:18 in the Hebrew text and KJV?
opt1: "silence"
opt2: "despair"
opt3: "darkness"
opt4: "the grave"
correct: "darkness"
explanation: Psalm 88 is the only psalm in the Psalter that ends without a resolution of praise, joy, or deliverance; its final word is 'darkness' (Hebrew machshak - 'mine acquaintance into darkness'). Psalm 88:18 (KJV) - "Lover and friend hast thou put far away from me, and mine acquaintance into darkness."

question: What makes Psalm 88 completely unique among all the lament psalms in the entire Psalter?
opt1: It is the only psalm that curses the day of the author's birth like Job
opt2: It is the only psalm that directly denies the existence of the afterlife
opt3: It is the only psalm that was forbidden from being chanted in the Second Temple
opt4: It is the only psalm that contains no transition to thanksgiving, praise, or joy; it remains enveloped in unrelieved darkness from beginning to end
correct: It is the only psalm that contains no transition to thanksgiving, praise, or joy; it remains enveloped in unrelieved darkness from beginning to end
explanation: While all other laments eventually pivot into praise or confidence, Psalm 88 maintains raw, unresolved darkness, validating the profound biblical reality that authentic faith can cry out in ongoing agony. Psalm 88:18 (KJV) - "Lover and friend hast thou put far away from me, and mine acquaintance into darkness."

question: Who is identified as the author in the detailed superscription of Psalm 88?
opt1: Heman the Ezrahite (a renowned sage and master musician, 1 Kings 4:31; 1 Chronicles 15:17-19)
opt2: Ethan the Ezrahite
opt3: Jeduthun the chief musician
opt4: Asaph the seer
correct: Heman the Ezrahite (a renowned sage and master musician, 1 Kings 4:31; 1 Chronicles 15:17-19)
explanation: Heman the Ezrahite was a legendary wise man (compared with Solomon in 1 Kings 4:31) and a primary choir master in David's tabernacle. Psalm 88:Title (KJV) - "A Song or Psalm for the sons of Korah, to the chief Musician upon Mahalath Leannoth, Maschil of Heman the Ezrahite."

question: What twin covenant attributes of God will the psalmist sing of and establish for all generations in Psalm 89:1-2?
opt1: "I will sing of the mercies of the LORD for ever: with my mouth will I make known thy faithfulness to all generations. For I have said, Mercy shall be built up for ever: thy faithfulness shalt thou establish in the very heavens."
opt2: "I will declare the righteousness of the Lord in the congregation: thy salvation shall endure throughout all ages;"
opt3: "My tongue shall celebrate the holiness of God: thy truth shalt thou plant like the cedar of Lebanon;"
opt4: "I will praise the power of the Almighty day and night: thy glory shalt thou display among all nations;"
correct: "I will sing of the mercies of the LORD for ever: with my mouth will I make known thy faithfulness to all generations. For I have said, Mercy shall be built up for ever: thy faithfulness shalt thou establish in the very heavens."
explanation: The overarching dual theme of Psalm 89: God's steadfast covenant mercies (hesed) and His unwavering veracity/faithfulness (emunah), established eternally in the heavens. Psalm 89:1-2 (KJV) - "I will sing of the mercies of the LORD for ever: with my mouth will I make known thy faithfulness to all generations. For I have said, Mercy shall be built up for ever: thy faithfulness shalt thou establish in the very heavens."

question: What unconditional royal covenant sworn with an oath is recorded in Psalm 89:3-4?
opt1: "I have sworn unto Abraham my friend, and confirmed my oath unto Isaac: Thy seed shall be as the stars of heaven. Selah;"
opt2: "I have made a covenant with my chosen, I have sworn unto David my servant, Thy seed will I establish for ever, and build up thy throne to all generations. Selah."
opt3: "I have established a statute with Judah my lawgiver: The sceptre shall not depart from between his feet for ever. Selah;"
opt4: "I have anointed Solomon my son, and promised unto his house: An everlasting kingdom of peace and righteousness. Selah;"
correct: "I have made a covenant with my chosen, I have sworn unto David my servant, Thy seed will I establish for ever, and build up thy throne to all generations. Selah."
explanation: God's unilateral, unconditional covenant with David (2 Samuel 7): guaranteeing that his royal seed and throne will endure throughout all perpetual generations. Psalm 89:3-4 (KJV) - "I have made a covenant with my chosen, I have sworn unto David my servant, Thy seed will I establish for ever, and build up thy throne to all generations. Selah."

question: What foundational pillars uphold God's heavenly throne, and what attributes go before His face in Psalm 89:14?
opt1: "Righteousness and holiness are the pillars of thy sanctuary: grace and salvation attend thy steps"
opt2: "Power and majesty are the foundation of thy kingdom: lovingkindness and peace herald thy presence"
opt3: "Justice and judgment are the habitation of thy throne: mercy and truth shall go before thy face."
opt4: "Eternity and glory surround thy seat: judgment and truth proceed from thy mouth"
correct: "Justice and judgment are the habitation of thy throne: mercy and truth shall go before thy face."
explanation: God's cosmic government rests upon the immovable twin moral pillars of Justice and Judgment, escorted wherever He moves by Mercy and Truth. Psalm 89:14 (KJV) - "Justice and judgment are the habitation of thy throne: mercy and truth shall go before thy face."

question: What beatitude belongs to the people who recognize the festival trumpet blast in Psalm 89:15?
opt1: "Blessed are the tribes that assemble in Zion: they shall behold the beauty of the holy temple"
opt2: "Blessed is the congregation that obeyeth the law: they shall flourish under the shadow of his wings"
opt3: "Blessed are the saints that offer sacrifices: they shall rejoice in the horn of David"
opt4: "Blessed is the people that know the joyful sound: they shall walk, O LORD, in the light of thy countenance."
correct: "Blessed is the people that know the joyful sound: they shall walk, O LORD, in the light of thy countenance."
explanation: The 'joyful sound' (Hebrew teruah) is the festival trumpet shofar blast heralding jubilee, festival communion, and royal victory, walking in the radiant favor of God's face. Psalm 89:15 (KJV) - "Blessed is the people that know the joyful sound: they shall walk, O LORD, in the light of thy countenance."

question: What divine election and sacred anointing of David are recalled in Psalm 89:20-21?
opt1: "I have found David my servant; with my holy oil have I anointed him: With whom my hand shall be established: mine arm also shall strengthen him."
opt2: "I have chosen the son of Jesse; with the horn of salvation have I consecrated his crown: my right hand shall defend him;"
opt3: "I have called David from the sheepfold; with royal garments have I clothed his majesty: my angels shall fight for him;"
opt4: "I have set David upon Mount Zion; with the sceptre of righteousness have I established his seed: my power shall uphold him;"
correct: "I have found David my servant; with my holy oil have I anointed him: With whom my hand shall be established: mine arm also shall strengthen him."
explanation: God sovereignly sought and 'found' David, consecrating him with holy anointing oil, promising the constant upholding power of His omnipotent hand and arm. Psalm 89:20-21 (KJV) - "I have found David my servant; with my holy oil have I anointed him: With whom my hand shall be established: mine arm also shall strengthen him."

question: What supreme Messianic title of preeminence above all earthly monarchs is bestowed in Psalm 89:27?
opt1: "Behold, I will crown him King of kings, and establish his dominion over all nations"
opt2: "Yea, I will make him the prince of peace, and exalt his throne above the stars of heaven"
opt3: "Also I will make him my firstborn, higher than the kings of the earth."
opt4: "Verily he shall be my beloved son, and inherit the uttermost parts of the earth"
correct: "Also I will make him my firstborn, higher than the kings of the earth."
explanation: The Davidic King is designated God's 'firstborn' (bekhor - supreme in rank, honor, and inheritance), prefiguring Jesus Christ, the 'firstborn from the dead' and 'prince of the kings of the earth' (Col 1:15; Rev 1:5). Psalm 89:27 (KJV) - "Also I will make him my firstborn, higher than the kings of the earth."

question: How does God reconcile disciplinary chastisement with His unconditional covenant fidelity in Psalm 89:30-34?
opt1: "Then will I cast them into captivity, and give their kingdom to the heathen. Yet after seventy years will I restore Zion;"
opt2: "Then will I smite their princes with pestilence, and scatter their seed. But for Abraham's sake I will show mercy;"
opt3: "Then will I take away their crown, and burn their cities. Nevertheless I will raise up the horn of David in the latter days;"
opt4: "Then will I visit their transgression with the rod, and their iniquity with stripes. Nevertheless my lovingkindness will I not utterly take from him, nor suffer my faithfulness to fail. My covenant will I not break, nor alter the thing that is gone out of my lips."
correct: "Then will I visit their transgression with the rod, and their iniquity with stripes. Nevertheless my lovingkindness will I not utterly take from him, nor suffer my faithfulness to fail. My covenant will I not break, nor alter the thing that is gone out of my lips."
explanation: Paternal discipline without covenant cancellation: rebellious Davidic sons will be scourged with disciplinary stripes, yet God's hesed remains immutable; He will never break His sworn oath. Psalm 89:33-34 (KJV) - "Nevertheless my lovingkindness will I not utterly take from him, nor suffer my faithfulness to fail. My covenant will I not break, nor alter the thing that is gone out of my lips."

question: What tragic historical collapse of the Davidic monarchy provokes the psalmist's agonizing lament in Psalm 89:38-39?
opt1: "But thou hast cast off and abhorred, thou hast been wroth with thine anointed. Thou hast made void the covenant of thy servant: thou hast profaned his crown by casting it to the ground."
opt2: "Yet the crown of Solomon is fallen, and the temple burned with fire: thou hast delivered the ark into the hands of Babylon;"
opt3: "Behold, the armies of Judah have fled, and our king is bound in bronze chains: thou hast forsaken Mount Zion;"
opt4: "For the throne of David is overturned, and his palaces are brought to ruin: thou hast forgotten thine oath;"
correct: "But thou hast cast off and abhorred, thou hast been wroth with thine anointed. Thou hast made void the covenant of thy servant: thou hast profaned his crown by casting it to the ground."
explanation: The heartbreaking paradox of the Babylonian exile: the sworn eternal covenant seemed shattered when God permitted the Davidic crown to be trampled in the dust. Psalm 89:38-39 (KJV) - "But thou hast cast off and abhorred, thou hast been wroth with thine anointed. Thou hast made void the covenant of thy servant: thou hast profaned his crown by casting it to the ground."

question: What doxology concludes Book III of the Psalter in Psalm 89:52?
opt1: "Praise the Lord from the heavens; praise him in the heights; Amen, and Amen."
opt2: "Blessed be the LORD for evermore. Amen, and Amen."
opt3: "Glory be to the Holy One of Israel throughout all generations; Amen, and Amen."
opt4: "Exalted be the King of glory from everlasting to everlasting; Amen, and Amen."
correct: "Blessed be the LORD for evermore. Amen, and Amen."
explanation: Even amid the wreckage of Jerusalem and the apparent defeat of the royal line, Book III closes with an unyielding doxology of faith: 'Blessed be the LORD for evermore. Amen, and Amen.' Psalm 89:52 (KJV) - "Blessed be the LORD for evermore. Amen, and Amen."

question: Who authored Psalm 89 according to its superscription?
opt1: Maschil of Asaph
opt2: A Psalm of David
opt3: Maschil of Ethan the Ezrahite
opt4: A Song of the Sons of Korah
correct: Maschil of Ethan the Ezrahite
explanation: Ethan the Ezrahite, along with Heman, was one of the legendary sages of Israel noted for musical and theological brilliance (1 Kings 4:31). Psalm 89:Title (KJV) - "Maschil of Ethan the Ezrahite."

question: What opening confession of God as Israel's eternal dwelling place opens Book IV in Psalm 90:1-2?
opt1: "O Lord of hosts, how amiable are thy tabernacles: from the foundation of the world thou art our fortress;"
opt2: "Lord, thou hast been our dwelling place in all generations. Before the mountains were brought forth, or ever thou hadst formed the earth and the world, even from everlasting to everlasting, thou art God."
opt3: "The Lord our God is an everlasting rock: before the heavens were stretched out, thou reignest King of glory;"
opt4: "In the shadow of the Almighty have we dwelt: before the hills were established, thou art the Holy One of Jacob;"
correct: "Lord, thou hast been our dwelling place in all generations. Before the mountains were brought forth, or ever thou hadst formed the earth and the world, even from everlasting to everlasting, thou art God."
explanation: Moses begins Book IV by celebrating God's aseity and eternity: while nomadic Israel wandered in tents with no fixed address for forty years, God Himself was their timeless home. Psalm 90:1-2 (KJV) - "Lord, thou hast been our dwelling place in all generations. Before the mountains were brought forth, or ever thou hadst formed the earth and the world, even from everlasting to everlasting, thou art God."

question: How does God's timeless eternity view a thousand human years in Psalm 90:4?
opt1: "For a millennium is as a fleeting breath, and as a drop of water in the great ocean"
opt2: "For ten thousand years are as morning dew, and as a shadow that vanisheth before the sun"
opt3: "For all the ages of the world are but as a single day, and as a moment in the heavens"
opt4: "For a thousand years in thy sight are but as yesterday when it is past, and as a watch in the night."
correct: "For a thousand years in thy sight are but as yesterday when it is past, and as a watch in the night."
explanation: To the eternal Creator, a millennium of human history shrinks down to a single yesterday that has already slipped away, or a brief 4-hour night watch (quoted in 2 Peter 3:8). Psalm 90:4 (KJV) - "For a thousand years in thy sight are but as yesterday when it is past, and as a watch in the night."

question: What botanical metaphor depicts the rapid fleeting cycle of human life in Psalm 90:5-6?
opt1: "in the morning they are like grass which groweth up. In the morning it flourisheth, and groweth up; in the evening it is cut down, and withereth."
opt2: "they are as the blossom of the almond tree: blooming in the spring, and falling to the dust before autumn"
opt3: "they are like the flower of the field: beautiful at dawn, and scorched by the desert wind at noon"
opt4: "they are as a leaf driven by the tempest: flourishing in the rain, and consumed by the fire in a moment"
correct: "in the morning they are like grass which groweth up. In the morning it flourisheth, and groweth up; in the evening it is cut down, and withereth."
explanation: Human existence is compressed into a single 12-hour vegetative cycle: sprouting fresh and green in the morning dew, cut down by the scythe and completely withered by evening dusk. Psalm 90:5-6 (KJV) - "in the morning they are like grass which groweth up. In the morning it flourisheth, and groweth up; in the evening it is cut down, and withereth."

question: Where does God place our secret sins and iniquities in Psalm 90:8?
opt1: "Thou hast recorded our transgressions in thy book, and weighed our iniquities in the balances of judgment"
opt2: "Thou hast set our iniquities before thee, our secret sins in the light of thy countenance."
opt3: "Thou hast brought our secret wickedness into the open court, and judged our deeds before the congregation"
opt4: "Thou hast exposed our hidden faults before heaven, and visited our backslidings with stripes"
correct: "Thou hast set our iniquities before thee, our secret sins in the light of thy countenance."
explanation: Nothing escapes divine omniscience: human sins hidden from public view are placed directly into the brilliant, unshielded spotlight of God's holy countenance. Psalm 90:8 (KJV) - "Thou hast set our iniquities before thee, our secret sins in the light of thy countenance."

question: What standard mortal lifespan and character of human existence are defined in Psalm 90:10?
opt1: "The measure of man's days is seventy years; and if he reach eighty in honor, yet are his steps full of vanity;"
opt2: "Our life span is as sixty years; and if by great health it be seventy, yet are our years spent in tears and trouble;"
opt3: "The days of our years are threescore years and ten; and if by reason of strength they be fourscore years, yet is their strength labour and sorrow; for it is soon cut off, and we fly away."
opt4: "Man that is born of a woman hath eighty years; yet his days are as a passing shadow, and he goeth down to the dust;"
correct: "The days of our years are threescore years and ten; and if by reason of strength they be fourscore years, yet is their strength labour and sorrow; for it is soon cut off, and we fly away."
explanation: Moses defines normal human longevity as seventy years ('threescore years and ten') or eighty ('fourscore') for the robust; yet even that peak is characterized by toil and grief, soon terminating in swift departure. Psalm 90:10 (KJV) - "The days of our years are threescore years and ten; and if by reason of strength they be fourscore years, yet is their strength labour and sorrow; for it is soon cut off, and we fly away."

question: What famous prayer for perspective and spiritual wisdom is recorded in Psalm 90:12?
opt1: "Lord, show us the measure of our frailty, that we may seek thy righteousness all our days;"
opt2: "Instruct our souls in the brevity of life, that we may walk uprightly before thy holy face;"
opt3: "Teach us to ponder the end of our years, that our minds may be established in thy fear;"
opt4: "So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom."
correct: "So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom."
explanation: A master prayer for daily living: consciously calculating the finite brevity of our days compels the heart to turn away from folly and cultivate true, eternal divine wisdom. Psalm 90:12 (KJV) - "So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom."

question: What early morning petition for divine satisfaction fuels a lifetime of gladness in Psalm 90:14?
opt1: "O satisfy us early with thy mercy; that we may rejoice and be glad all our days."
opt2: "Fill our souls at daybreak with thy lovingkindness; that our tongue may sing of thy righteousness continually"
opt3: "Refresh our spirits in the morning watch with thy grace; that we may celebrate thy salvation without ceasing"
opt4: "Satisfy our hunger with the bread of heaven; that our heart may boast in the God of our fathers"
correct: "O satisfy us early with thy mercy; that we may rejoice and be glad all our days."
explanation: Starting each day anchored in God's steadfast covenant mercy (hesed) provides deep inner contentment that sustains radiant joy throughout all of life's trials. Psalm 90:14 (KJV) - "O satisfy us early with thy mercy; that we may rejoice and be glad all our days."

question: What reciprocal proportion of joy corresponding to past suffering is requested in Psalm 90:15?
opt1: "Restore unto us double joy for all our tears, and multiply our peace according to our sorrow"
opt2: "Make us glad according to the days wherein thou hast afflicted us, and the years wherein we have seen evil."
opt3: "Give us rejoicing in Zion according to our weeping in exile, and comfort us on every side"
opt4: "Crown our heads with gladness according to our afflictions, and blot out the memory of our grief"
correct: "Make us glad according to the days wherein thou hast afflicted us, and the years wherein we have seen evil."
explanation: Moses prays that the coming seasons of divine joy and blessing will be equal in measure to the grueling forty years of desert affliction and grief they had endured. Psalm 90:15 (KJV) - "Make us glad according to the days wherein thou hast afflicted us, and the years wherein we have seen evil."

question: What double plea for divine favor and permanent vocational impact concludes Psalm 90:17?
opt1: "And let the glory of the Almighty cover our sanctuary: and prosper thou the way of thy chosen seed for ever"
opt2: "And let the peace of God dwell in our borders: and confirm thou the heritage of our fathers throughout all generations"
opt3: "And let the beauty of the LORD our God be upon us: and establish thou the work of our hands upon us; yea, the work of our hands establish thou it."
opt4: "And let the lovingkindness of the King rest upon our families: and bless thou the labor of our hands in Zion"
correct: "And let the beauty of the LORD our God be upon us: and establish thou the work of our hands upon us; yea, the work of our hands establish thou it."
explanation: The ultimate benediction: praying that the pleasantness / radiant beauty (no'am) of Yahweh rest upon mortal humans, giving enduring, permanent significance to their fleeting earthly labors. Psalm 90:17 (KJV) - "And let the beauty of the LORD our God be upon us: and establish thou the work of our hands upon us; yea, the work of our hands establish thou it."

question: Who is the unique author of Psalm 90 identified in its superscription?
opt1: David the son of Jesse
opt2: Asaph the chief musician
opt3: Solomon the king of Israel
opt4: Moses the man of God
correct: Moses the man of God
explanation: Psalm 90 is the only psalm in the entire Psalter composed by Moses, making it the oldest psalm in the Bible, reflecting the forty years of wandering in the wilderness as a generation died off. Psalm 90:Title (KJV) - "A Prayer of Moses the man of God."
